title: A/B arbitration
text: UDP can lose packets, so some exchanges send every packet twice, on two separate multicast feeds. Arbitration is how the handler merges them back into one clean stream.

title: Two lines
text: CME's documentation for its MDP 3.0 feed puts it plainly. All packets are sent through both feed A and feed B, and the two should be used for arbitration. A packet lost on one line can still arrive on the other. And whichever copy lands first, you get to use it.

title: One counter
text: The rule is simple, because both lines carry the same sequence numbers. Keep a single counter: the next sequence you expect. A message that matches it is delivered, whichever line it came on. A copy you have already delivered is a duplicate, and is dropped. A message beyond the counter means both lines have a hole so far, so it is held, and the gap logic takes over. This is the same counter that gap detection uses. So arbitration costs one compare per message, and the gap logic never needs to know there were two lines.

title: In the lab
text: The lab's feed has a single line, but its sequencer already contains the arbitration rule. This is accept, from the MoldUDP64 sequencer in libs/mold. Equal to expected: deliver it and advance. Below expected: count a duplicate and return. Above: hold it until the gap fills. Feed both lines into one sequencer, with the same session and numbering, and duplicates fall out for free. The lab's fault injector sends duplicate packets on purpose, to test exactly this path. In one of the lab's live-feed runs, the sequencer dropped 5,240 duplicate messages, and the book saw no duplicate order references.

title: Worked example
text: Messages 1001 to 1006. Line A loses 1003 and 1005. Line B loses 1002, and in this example runs 40 microseconds behind. A delivers 1001 and 1002 straight away. 1003 exists only on B, so the handler waits for B's copy. A's 1004 arrived first, but it is held, and goes out right behind B's 1003. The same happens for 1005 and 1006. The output is complete, and no retransmission request was sent.

title: What to watch
text: What do pros watch? Skew: every hole on the fast line costs you the slow line's delay, so measure the gap between the lines. Count, per line, how often each one delivered first; if one line almost never wins, something on its path is slow. A dead line: alert when one feed goes quiet, even while the other carries you. And a message lost on both lines. That is a real gap, and the next video is about it.

title: Takeaway
text: Two lines, one counter. Take the first copy of each sequence number, drop the second, and only ask for a retransmission when both lines missed it.
